          DEMAND A PUCT AUDIT OF SEMPRA AND ONCOR'S
                        INTERACTIONS
 On September 19, 2026, Texas Scorecard reported that critics contend the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT),
 the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), and Oncor transformed what began as a regional reliability initiative
 into what those critics characterize as a de facto statewide 765-kV transmission plan without an explicit legislative vote.

    That controversy raises another important question: Has the PUCT adequately examined the relationship
    between Oncor and its majority owner, Sempra, as billions of dollars of new Texas transmission
    investment have been proposed?

 THE SEMPRA-ONCOR RING FENCE
 When the PUCT approved Sempra Energy's 2018 acquisition of an indirect majority interest in Oncor, it did so subject
 to extensive regulatory commitments designed to preserve Oncor's independence from Sempra.

 Those commitments are contained in PUCT Docket No. 47675, Joint Report and Application of Oncor Electric Delivery
 Company LLC and Sempra Energy for Regulatory Approvals Pursuant to PURA §§14.101, 39.262, and 39.915. The
 Commission issued its Final Order on March 8, 2018.

 Oncor continues to describe itself as governed by a 13-member board consisting of seven disinterested directors, two
 Sempra-designated directors, two Texas Transmission-designated directors, and two current or former Oncor
 officers.

 The Final Order also imposed substantive governance protections. Among them, Oncor's board cannot be overruled by
 Sempra or its subsidiaries on specified matters including dividend policy, debt issuance, capital expenditures, operations
 and maintenance expenditures, management and service fees, and appointment or removal of board members. Certain
 significant capital and operating budget changes require approval by a majority of the disinterested directors.

 The financial-separation requirements include arm's-length and separate-books-and-records commitments. The Final
 Order establishes Commission access to Sempra books and records in connection with the specified ring-fencing and
 affiliate-transaction audit/review requirements. That provision should not be read as unlimited authority over every
 Sempra-Oncor interaction; it is important because it provides an express regulatory basis for review within the scope of
 the commitments imposed by the Order.

 Oncor's current SEC disclosure makes the purpose and effect of these protections unusually clear: as a result of the
 ring-fencing measures, "Sempra does not control Oncor", and Sempra's ability to direct Oncor's management,
 policies, operations, asset deployment, dividends, strategic planning, and other important corporate matters is limited.

    That creates the central governance question: Where does Sempra's oversight of its investment end and
    independently governed Oncor decision-making begin?

 ONCOR'S REQUIRED COMPLIANCE REPORTS
 The Final Order required Oncor to report annually on compliance with the regulatory commitments for five years. The
 Commission established PUCT Project No. 48119 - Compliance Reports of Oncor Electric Delivery Company
 Regarding Regulatory Commitments in Docket No. 47675.

 Interchange Item 4 - March 11, 2019: 2018 Annual Compliance Report.
 Item 5 - March 9, 2020: 2019 Annual Compliance Report.
 Item 6 - March 9, 2021: 2020 Annual Compliance Report.
 Item 7 - March 9, 2022: 2021 Annual Compliance Report.
 Item 8 - March 9, 2023: 2022 Annual Compliance Report.

 Those five reports appear to satisfy the five-year reporting obligation. Filing compliance reports, however, is not the
 same thing as an independent examination of the underlying communications, board materials, approvals, books and
 records.



PUCT Docket No. 47675 | PUCT Project No. 48119                                                                           Page 1
  WHY THE SEPTEMBER 2025 DALLAS TRIP DESERVES SCRUTINY
 An exchange during Sempra's November 5, 2025 third-quarter earnings call provides a concrete reason to examine
 how the ring fence operated during development of the 765-kV strategy.

 Goldman Sachs analyst Carly Davenport asked Sempra Chairman and CEO Jeffrey Martin about transmission
 expansion in Texas, equipment and supply-chain availability, and confidence in executing a growing capital plan.

 Martin responded that in September Sempra took its Board of Directors to Dallas and said the number-one issue was the
 ability to deliver on growth plans and the strength of the supply chain. He then said Governor Greg Abbott joined the
 Sempra Board for a private three-hour dinner while Sempra continued to conduct due diligence on what Martin called
 the company's "growth case in Texas."

 The existence of the dinner does not establish improper conduct, does not establish what was discussed at the dinner,
 and does not establish a ring-fencing violation. It does, however, make the underlying records relevant to understanding
 the boundary between Sempra's investment oversight and Oncor's independent governance.

 THE MIDLOTHIAN VISIT
 Martin also said Sempra took its "entire board" on a field visit to Oncor's Midlothian supply center. He described the
 facility as a sophisticated, digitally driven distribution center supporting Oncor's supply chain across its five-year plan as
 well as storm-recovery operations.

 The significance is straightforward: according to Sempra's own CEO, this was not simply a social trip. Sempra's Board
 was examining Oncor's ability to execute its growth plan and the supply chain supporting that plan.

 THE 765-kV PROCUREMENT DISCUSSION
 The earnings-call discussion then moved directly to 765-kV equipment. Martin asked Oncor CEO Allen Nye about
 Oncor's efforts in Asia and Europe to address 765-kV equipment "well before it became something that crystallized
 for the state."

 Nye confirmed that Oncor had been working with suppliers in Asia and Europe and described the advance
 commitments Oncor had made to position itself to execute the 765-kV plan.

 That wording matters. The public exchange establishes advance procurement activity, but it should not be characterized
 as proof that a particular regulatory authorization was required or granted. The proper audit question is what
 commitments were made, when they were made, what corporate approvals were required and obtained, and what
 regulatory approvals, if any, were required at that stage.

 THE GOVERNANCE TENSION IS DOCUMENTED BY THE COMPANIES THEMSELVES
 Oncor tells the SEC that Sempra does not control Oncor and that the ring fence limits Sempra's ability to direct Oncor's
 strategic planning and other important corporate actions. Sempra, meanwhile, publicly presents Oncor's Texas capital
 expansion as an important component of Sempra's growth strategy.

 Sempra's November 2025 business update said Oncor expected to be responsible for more than half of the
 investment in ERCOT's 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan and anticipated a more than 30% increase
 in its roll-forward 2026-2030 base capital plan.

    There is nothing inherently improper about Sempra monitoring the performance of a major investment.
    The regulatory question is narrower and more important: did the documented governance processes
    preserve the distinction between Sempra's investment oversight and Oncor's independently governed
    strategic decision-making while the 765-kV strategy and associated capital commitments were being
    developed?

 WHO WAS THERE?




PUCT Docket No. 47675 | PUCT Project No. 48119                                                                             Page 2
  Martin stated that the entire Sempra Board participated in the Midlothian field visit. The publicly available earnings-call
 transcript does not individually identify the attendees at the private dinner with Governor Abbott. Therefore, the dinner
 attendees - and whether Oncor executives, Texas officials, consultants, lobbyists or others were present - should be
 established from records rather than assumed.

 Relevant records could include the Governor's calendar and scheduling records; Sempra and Oncor calendars;
 invitations; visitor and security records; expense and travel records; emails and text messages concerning the event;
 agendas and briefing materials; and records identifying the location, hosts and attendees.

 QUESTIONS AN INDEPENDENT REVIEW SHOULD ANSWER
    What information concerning the development of Oncor's 765-kV strategy was provided to Sempra or
    Sempra's Board; when was it provided; and were decisions concerning Oncor's 765-kV strategy,
    procurement, capital budgets, or execution plans presented to or approved by Oncor's disinterested
    directors?

    Did Sempra or its Board provide direction, recommendations, requests, approvals, targets, or other input
    concerning Oncor's 765-kV strategy, capital investment, procurement, or execution schedule; and if so,
    how were those interactions documented and treated under the ring-fencing requirements?

 What 765-kV equipment commitments had Oncor made before the plan had "crystallized for the state," as Martin
 described it? When were those commitments made, what corporate approvals were required and obtained, and what
 regulatory approvals, if any, were required at that stage?

 What information concerning Oncor's five-year capital plan was presented to Sempra's Board during the Dallas meeting
 and Midlothian tour?

 What exactly was discussed during the private three-hour dinner involving Governor Abbott and the Sempra Board, and
 who attended? Did the discussions involve Oncor, Texas transmission expansion, ERCOT transmission planning, the
 765-kV system, regulatory matters, capital investment or Sempra's Texas growth strategy?

 Were relevant Oncor capital budgets and transmission strategies reviewed and approved in accordance with the
 governance requirements applicable to the disinterested directors? Were affiliate transactions and information
 exchanges conducted at arm's length and properly documented?

 PUCT ALREADY ESTABLISHED A BASIS TO REVIEW COMPLIANCE
 The Commission need not presume a violation in order to examine whether its safeguards worked. Finding of Fact No.
 69 in Docket No. 47675 should be read in its exact context: the Final Order establishes access to Sempra books and
 records as necessary to facilitate Commission audit or review in connection with the specified affiliate-transaction and
 ring-fencing requirements.

 For any submission to commissioners, legislators or investigators, the Final Order itself should be treated as the
 controlling legal text rather than relying solely on a summary of Finding 69.

 The five annual compliance reports required under Project No. 48119 are publicly identifiable. This review has not
 identified a comparable publicly available filing documenting a comprehensive PUCT audit of Sempra-Oncor
 interactions under these ring-fencing provisions. That statement is intentionally limited to the public record reviewed;
 it is not proof that no other review ever occurred.

 TEXANS DESERVE AN INDEPENDENT REVIEW
 The strongest case for review is not an allegation that Sempra violated the ring fence. The public record cited here does
 not establish that.

 Rather, the record shows that the PUCT imposed specific safeguards to preserve Oncor's independent governance;
 Sempra says its Board traveled to Texas to evaluate Oncor's growth execution, toured Oncor's supply-chain operation,
 met privately for three hours with Governor Abbott while examining Sempra's Texas growth case, and publicly discussed
 Oncor's advance efforts to secure 765-kV equipment. At the same time, Oncor represents that Sempra does not control



PUCT Docket No. 47675 | PUCT Project No. 48119                                                                            Page 3
  Oncor's strategic planning.

    Those facts provide a concrete basis for the PUCT to examine the underlying records and determine
    whether the ring-fencing safeguards operated as intended.

 An independent review should examine Sempra-Oncor communications; Oncor and Oncor Holdings board minutes and
 voting records; Sempra Board materials relating to Oncor; disinterested-director approvals; capital-budget decisions;
 affiliate transactions; financing and distributions; records concerning the September 2025 Dallas trip; the Midlothian
 supply-center visit; the private three-hour dinner involving Governor Abbott; advance 765-kV procurement commitments;
 and communications concerning the Permian Basin and 765-kV STEP transmission plans.

 The purpose of an audit is not to supply the answer in advance. It is to let the records answer the question.

    The PUCT required a ring fence for a reason. Texans deserve to know whether that fence has operated as
    intended.
